name: Protein Structure Prediction
title: Protein Structure Prediction
answer: Protein structure prediction is the computational task of taking an amino acid sequence and producing a three dimensional model of how that chain folds. In drug discovery it sits upstream of docking, molecular dynamics and design work, because a structure is often the starting point for asking how a small molecule might bind. The field covers single domains, multi chain complexes, and increasingly the flexibility and alternative conformations that matter for real binding sites. It is distinct from experimental structure determination by X-ray crystallography, cryo electron microscopy or NMR, though the two are used together.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Protein structure prediction is the computational task of taking an amino acid sequence and producing a three dimensional model of how that chain folds. In drug discovery it sits upstream of docking, molecular dynamics and design work, because a structure is often the starting point for asking how a small molecule might bind. The field covers single domains, multi chain complexes, and increasingly the flexibility and alternative conformations that matter for real binding sites. It is distinct from experimental structure determination by X-ray crystallography, cryo electron microscopy or NMR, though the two are used together.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on graphics processors, since the dominant models are deep neural networks trained on large sets of known structures and sequences. Training and inference both depend on public repositories such as the Protein Data Bank and sequence databases like UniProt, alongside multiple sequence alignments built from large sequence collections. Tooling is commonly distributed as open source packages, with AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold among the widely used systems, and ColabFold offering a more accessible route to running them. Storage and compute for alignment generation can be as demanding as the model itself.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pipeline starts with a sequence, searches for homologous sequences, and builds a multiple sequence alignment whose covariation patterns hint at which residues are close in space. A neural network then predicts distances, angles or directly coordinates, often using attention over the alignment and, where available, a structural template. The output is a set of candidate models with per residue confidence estimates, which practitioners inspect before using the model for anything downstream. Refinement, energy minimisation and comparison against experimental data are common next steps, and a prediction is treated as a hypothesis rather than a solved structure.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Predicted models are not experimental measurements, and the confidence scores attached to them are part of how they should be read and reported. Provenance matters: which sequence, which database release, which model version and which parameters produced a given file all affect reproducibility. Licensing varies across tools and their weights, and some uses, particularly commercial ones, carry terms that differ from the academic setting the models were often developed in. Where a prediction informs a patent filing, a clinical programme or a regulatory submission, the distinction between predicted and experimentally determined structure is usually documented explicitly.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward complexes, assemblies and conformational ensembles rather than single static chains, and toward models that incorporate experimental restraints and sparse data. Integration with design and simulation is deepening, so a predicted structure increasingly feeds directly into generative molecule design or into molecular dynamics rather than sitting as a separate artefact. Confidence estimation and error detection remain active areas, since knowing when a model is wrong is as useful as the model itself. How these predictions are validated, cited and licensed will keep shaping how far they can be relied on in regulated drug development.
